idiom_name: JVM template engines (Thymeleaf, FreeMarker) or kotlinx.html's typed HTML DSL
implementation_notes: Kotlin has no template syntax of its own: on the JVM it uses the same engines as Java (Thymeleaf, FreeMarker, Velocity), whose templates embed expressions and statements, so the classic structure is available through a library rather than through the language. The local replacement is kotlinx.html, a typed DSL in which markup is ordinary Kotlin function calls written to a Writer/Appendable or a DOM, and Ktor's HTML DSL is the same idea in framework form. Engine templates remain justified when markup must be editable outside the build or by authors who do not write Kotlin; otherwise a typed builder keeps the page under the compiler's eye, which is Kotlin's whole argument.
pitfalls: A builder DSL removes the template/code boundary entirely: loops, conditionals and data access become function calls, so the page is a program again - type-checked this time, but still a program that owns fetch and rendering together.

Coroutines do not penetrate a JVM engine's expression evaluation, so a suspending fetch cannot happen inside a Thymeleaf/FreeMarker template; resolve the data before rendering or the call blocks the request thread.
kotlinx.html can either stream to an Appendable or build a DOM; building the whole tree first costs memory proportional to the page, which matters for large pages and is easy to do accidentally.
With an engine, template expressions are untyped strings: field renames and nullability are invisible to the compiler, so the safety Kotlin normally provides stops at the `{{ ... }}` boundary.
